alignment.note: Greek opens with paratactic καὶ ἐάν ('and if'); the Peshitta fuses these into a single conditional particle ܘܐܢ, while the Vulgate recasts the connective as the relative-conditional Quod si, a stylistic Latin idiom that subordinates the clause to the preceding context rather than coordinating it.

Greek expresses 'your eye' analytically with article + noun + enclitic genitive (ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου); the Vulgate parallels this with oculus tuus, whereas Syriac employs the synthetic pronominal suffix ܥܝܢܟ, a single morphological word for the same phrase.
σκανδαλίζῃ σε / ܡܟܫܠܐ ܠܟ / scandalizat te.

Greek ἔκβαλε ('cast out') and Latin ejice both denote violent expulsion; the Syriac ܚܨܝܗ derives from a root meaning 'pluck/tear out', a slightly more graphic lexeme reflecting the physical extraction of the offending eye.

The Greek pronominal object αὐτόν ('it') is rendered in Latin by eum followed by editorial colon punctuation; the Peshitta omits the explicit object pronoun entirely, the verbal suffix on ܚܨܝܗ already encoding the object.
καλόν σέ ἐστιν / ܦܩܚ ܗܘ ܠܟ / bonum est tibi.

Greek uses the compact adjective μονόφθαλμον ('one-eyed') matched by Latin luscum; Syriac unpacks the same notion periphrastically as ܕܒܚܕܐ ܥܝܢܟ ('with one eye of yours'), preferring an analytic phrase over a single lexeme.

Greek 'into the kingdom of God' uses preposition + article + noun + genitive article + θεοῦ; Latin reduces the articles (in regnum Dei); Syriac compresses 'his kingdom of God' into ܠܡܠܟܘܬܗ ܕܐܠܗܐ with a proleptic pronominal suffix on 'kingdom', an idiomatic Syriac anticipatory possessive construction.

Greek 'having two eyes' is a participial phrase (δύο ὀφθαλμοὺς ἔχοντα) closely mirrored by Latin duos oculos habentem; Syriac recasts it as a circumstantial existential clause ܟܕ ܐܝܬ ܠܟ ܬܪܬܝܢ ܥܝܢܝܢ ('while there are to you two eyes'), the standard Syriac idiom for possession lacking a verb 'to have'.

Greek βληθῆναι and Latin mitti are passive infinitives ('to be cast'); the Syriac ܬܦܠ is an active intransitive ('that you fall'), shifting the agency from external casting to the subject's own falling into Gehenna.

Greek 'into the gehenna of the fire' is fully articulated (εἰς τὴν γέενναν τοῦ πυρός); Latin renders it anarthrously (in gehennam ignis); Syriac collapses preposition and noun into ܒܓܗܢܐ ܕܢܘܪܐ, an analytic genitive with ܕ, all three transmitting the same Semitic loan γέεννα/ܓܗܢܐ for the valley of Hinnom.
